name: Transfer Pricing
title: Transfer Pricing
answer: Transfer pricing is the set of rules and practices that govern how related entities within a multinational group price transactions with each other, including goods, services, royalties, loans, and cost allocations. It sits in tax and jurisdictional compliance because tax authorities in each country want to ensure that profits are not shifted artificially to low-tax jurisdictions. The work covers documentation, benchmarking, intercompany agreements, and dispute resolution. In an AI context, transfer pricing also touches how algorithms, data, and software licenses are valued when they cross borders.

sections.body: Transfer pricing is the set of rules and practices that govern how related entities within a multinational group price transactions with each other, including goods, services, royalties, loans, and cost allocations. It sits in tax and jurisdictional compliance because tax authorities in each country want to ensure that profits are not shifted artificially to low-tax jurisdictions. The work covers documentation, benchmarking, intercompany agreements, and dispute resolution. In an AI context, transfer pricing also touches how algorithms, data, and software licenses are valued when they cross borders.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Transfer pricing work runs on financial and tax data from ERP systems, legal entity ledgers, and intercompany accounting records. Practitioners rely on spreadsheets, tax provision software, and databases of comparable transactions, often from commercial benchmarking tools. AI-assisted systems can help extract and normalize data from contracts, invoices, and filings, then map transactions to the correct legal entities. The infrastructure must handle multiple currencies, tax years, and jurisdictions, and it must keep an audit trail for every adjustment.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The core method is to apply the arm's length principle, which asks what unrelated parties would have agreed to in comparable circumstances. Common approaches include the comparable uncontrolled price method, the resale price method, the cost plus method, the transactional net margin method, and the profit split method. Practitioners select the most appropriate method, identify comparables, and prepare local files, master files, and country by country reports. AI can speed up comparable searches, detect outliers, and draft documentation, but the judgment about comparability and risk remains with the tax professional.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Transfer pricing carries significant risk because tax authorities can challenge prices, impose penalties, and require retroactive adjustments. Provenance matters: every figure in a local file should trace back to a source system, a contract, or a benchmark study, and any AI-generated text or analysis must be reviewable and attributable. Rights over data, models, and intangibles are central, especially when the transfer pricing question involves intellectual property developed with AI. Governance also covers transfer pricing documentation retention, country by country reporting thresholds, and dispute resolution mechanisms such as mutual agreement procedures and advance pricing agreements.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Transfer pricing is moving toward more real-time monitoring, with tax authorities asking for granular data and automated exchange of information. AI is likely to take over more of the routine benchmarking and documentation work, while humans focus on controversy, policy design, and negotiation. The rise of digital services taxes and the global minimum tax will keep pressure on how profits are allocated across jurisdictions. For AI-specific assets, expect growing attention to how data, models, and compute are valued and where their economic ownership sits.
